title: Trees for sequences
objectives: Draw a probability tree and multiply along its branches
Label second-stage branches with conditional chances
Check a tree by adding its leaves, and prune branches with chance 0

screens.title: Trees for sequences
screens.prose: When one step follows another, a tree lays out every way things can go. Each branch carries a chance, and each route through the tree is one outcome.
A drawer holds 5 black socks and 3 white ones. You pull out two in the dark, one after the other. The tree has the first sock; the second-sock branches are blank.
screens.question: Fill in the four second-sock branches. Fractions are fine.

hints.text: After a black sock comes out, what is left in the drawer?
The top two blanks hang off the black first sock.
After black: 4 black and 3 white among 7. After white: 5 black and 2 white among 7.

feedback.correct: Each pair of branches is counted on what the first sock left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the socks left after each first sock: 7 in all.

byKey.r0c1: After a black sock, 4 black socks are left among 7.
byKey.r1c1: After a black sock, all 3 white socks are still there, among 7.
byKey.r2c1: After a white sock, all 5 black socks are still there, among 7.
byKey.r3c1: After a white sock, 2 white socks are left among 7.

explain.text: After a black sock, 4 black and 3 white are left: $\tfrac{4}{7}$ and $\tfrac{3}{7}$. After a white sock, 5 black and 2 white are left: $\tfrac{5}{7}$ and $\tfrac{2}{7}$. The second-stage numbers depend on the branch they hang from.

screens.prose: Each second-sock branch hangs off a first-sock branch. Tap a branch to mark it, and tap it again to clear it.
screens.question: Tap every branch on the way from the start to white, then white.

hints.text: Where does the route start, and which branch does it take first?
The route starts with the white first sock.

feedback.correct: Two branches: white first, then white again.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow one route from the start to the leaf white, then white.

byKey.leaf-only: You marked only the last branch. The route also passes through the white first sock.
byKey.all-white: You marked black, then white too. That is a different route, ending at a different leaf.
byKey.b: That branch is a black first sock. Your route starts with white.
byKey.b-b: That branch hangs off a black first sock. Your route starts with white.
byKey.b-w: That branch hangs off a black first sock. Your route starts with white.
byKey.w-b: That branch ends in a black second sock. Your route ends in white.

explain.text: You marked the white branch and the white branch after it. Together they make one route from the start to a leaf. Each route is one outcome of the two draws.

screens.prose: A route from the start to a leaf is a **path**: one outcome of both draws. Its chance comes from the branches along it.
screens.question: What is the chance of white, then white? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: Which two branches make up this path?
The path runs along white, then white again.
Multiply along the path: $\tfrac{3}{8} \times \tfrac{2}{7} = \tfrac{6}{56}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the chances on the two branches of the path.

byKey.unconditional: That is $\tfrac{3}{8} \times \tfrac{3}{8}$. The second branch is $\tfrac{2}{7}$: one white sock is already out.
byKey.added: You added along the path. Both draws must happen, so the chances multiply.
byKey.leaf-only: That is the second branch alone. Multiply by $\tfrac{3}{8}$ for the white first sock.

explain.text: A white sock comes first $\tfrac{3}{8}$ of the time, and $\tfrac{2}{7}$ of those continue with white. Multiplying along the path is the multiplication rule: $\tfrac{3}{8} \times \tfrac{2}{7} = \tfrac{6}{56} = \tfrac{3}{28}$.

screens.prose: Now every path. Multiply along each one, then add the four leaves.
screens.question: Fill in the chance of each path, then their total.

hints.text: Multiply along each path, as you did for white, then white.
Black, then black runs along the top of the tree.
$\tfrac{5}{8} \times \tfrac{4}{7} = \tfrac{20}{56}$. The others are $\tfrac{15}{56}$, $\tfrac{15}{56}$ and $\tfrac{6}{56}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply along each path, then add the four results.

byKey.r3c1: White, then white is $\tfrac{3}{8} \times \tfrac{2}{7}$, as on the last screen.
byKey.r4c1: Add the four path chances. Every pair of socks lands on exactly one path.

explain.text: The leaves are $\tfrac{20}{56}$, $\tfrac{15}{56}$, $\tfrac{15}{56}$ and $\tfrac{6}{56}$, which add to 1. Every outcome lies on exactly one path, so a tree's leaves always add to 1. That makes a quick check on your arithmetic.

screens.prose: A new drawer: 5 black socks and just 1 white. Again you pull out two, one after the other.
screens.question: Tap the branch you could remove without changing any chance.

hints.text: Is any branch impossible?
Look at the branches after the white sock.
After the white sock, no white is left: that branch has chance $\tfrac{0}{5}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the branch with chance 0.

byKey.white-first: A white first sock has chance $\tfrac{1}{6}$. Removing it would lose the path white, then black.
byKey.w: A white first sock has chance $\tfrac{1}{6}$. Removing it would lose the path white, then black.
byKey.b: A black first sock has chance $\tfrac{5}{6}$. It leads to most of the outcomes.
byKey.b-b: Black, then black has chance $\tfrac{4}{5}$ after a black sock. It happens often.
byKey.b-w: After a black sock, the white one is still in the drawer: $\tfrac{1}{5}$.
byKey.w-b: After the white sock, every sock left is black. That branch is certain.

explain.text: After the white sock, no white is left, so that branch has chance $\tfrac{0}{5} = 0$. Its leaf is $\tfrac{1}{6} \times 0 = 0$, so removing it changes nothing. That is the edge case: a zero branch can be pruned.

screens.prose: Back to 5 black and 3 white. This time you pull out three socks. One branch is blank.

state.caption: B is black and W is white. Branches off this path are folded away

screens.question: What is the chance of black, black, then white? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of black, black, then white

hints.text: What is left in the drawer after two black socks?
The blank branch hangs off black, then black.
After two black socks, 3 black and 3 white are left, so the branch is $\tfrac{3}{6}$. Multiply $\tfrac{5}{8} \times \tfrac{4}{7} \times \tfrac{3}{6}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the blank branch from what is left, then multiply along the path.

byKey.unconditional: You used $\tfrac{5}{8}$, $\tfrac{5}{8}$, $\tfrac{3}{8}$, as if each sock went back. Each stage is counted on what is left.
byKey.stale-third: You used $\tfrac{3}{8}$ for the third sock. After two black socks, 3 white sit among 6.
byKey.seven-left: You used $\tfrac{3}{7}$ for the third sock. Two socks are out, so 6 are left.

explain.text: Each stage is counted on what the stages before it left: $\tfrac{5}{8}$, then $\tfrac{4}{7}$, then $\tfrac{3}{6}$. The path multiplies to $\tfrac{60}{336} = \tfrac{5}{28}$. A deeper tree uses the same rule, one factor per stage.

screens.prose: Kim drew this tree for the first drawer: 5 black and 3 white, two socks, none put back. Her leaves add to $\tfrac{64}{64} = 1$, so she trusts it.
screens.question: What is the true chance of black, then white?

options.why: You trusted Kim's second branch, $\tfrac{3}{8}$. That is the chance before any sock left. After a black sock, 3 white sit among 7.
You added along the path, and got more than 1. Chances along a path multiply.
That is the second branch alone. Multiply by $\tfrac{5}{8}$ for the black first sock.

hints.text: Kim's second-stage numbers are the same after black as after white. Should they be?
Look at the branch black, then white.
After a black sock, 4 black and 3 white are left. So the branch is $\tfrac{3}{7}$, and the path is $\tfrac{5}{8} \times \tfrac{3}{7}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the second branch on what the black sock left, then multiply.

byKey.kim: You used Kim's $\tfrac{3}{8}$ on the second branch. That chance ignores the black sock already out.

explain.text: Kim wrote the first-draw chances on the second draw, as if the sock went back. Her leaves still add to 1, so that check cannot catch the slip. The true path is $\tfrac{5}{8} \times \tfrac{3}{7} = \tfrac{15}{56}$.

screens.prose: Each tree worked the same way. A first-stage branch carries $P(A)$. A branch hanging off $A$ carries $P(B \mid A)$, counted on what $A$ left. A path multiplies: $$P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$$ and the leaves add to 1.
screens.question: On the sock tree, what does the number on the branch white, then black stand for?

options.why: That is the chance with no news about the first sock. A branch hanging off white assumes the first was white.
That is the leaf at the end of the path. You get it by multiplying the two branches.
That turns the condition round. The branch is conditioned on the first sock, which comes earlier.

hints.text: Which sock is already known when you reach that branch?
The branch hangs off white, so the first sock is known to be white. It gives the chance of black next.

feedback.correct: A second-stage branch is conditional on the branch it hangs from.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what is already known at that point in the tree.

explain.text: The branch is reached only after a white first sock, so its $\tfrac{5}{7}$ is conditional on that. The leaf, $\tfrac{3}{8} \times \tfrac{5}{7}$, is the joint chance. With no news, a black second sock has chance $\tfrac{5}{8}$, a third number.

screens.prose: Why do the leaves always add to 1? Write $B_1$ for a black first sock, and $B_2$ or $W_2$ for the second. Start with the two leaves after a black first sock.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $P(B_1 \cap B_2) + P(B_1 \cap W_2)$, the two leaves after a black first sock
$= P(B_1)\,P(B_2 \mid B_1) + P(B_1)\,P(W_2 \mid B_1)$, multiply along each path
$= P(B_1)\,\big[P(B_2 \mid B_1) + P(W_2 \mid B_1)\big]$, take out the common factor
$= P(B_1)$, since the branches out of one node add to 1

hints.text: Which line is just the two leaves, before any rule is used?
The multiplication rule turns each leaf into a product.
Leaves, then products, then the common factor, then the bracket equals 1.

feedback.correct: Each line rewrites the one before it, with its reason.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the two leaves, then use one rule per line.

byKey.one: The bracket must appear before you can say it equals 1.
byKey.factor: You need the two products before you can take out the common factor.

explain.text: The two leaves after black add to $P(B_1)$, and the same steps after white give $P(W_1)$. Since $P(B_1) + P(W_1) = 1$, all four leaves add to 1. The proof only needs each node's branches to add to 1, which is why Kim's tree passed the check.

screens.prose: You place a limit order to buy. It fills with chance 0.6. Fills tend to come as the price falls. So a filled order is profitable at the close only 45% of the time. A buy made on any day, with no limit, is profitable at the close 52% of the time.

state.caption: An unfilled order has no profit branch: it is pruned

screens.question: What is the chance the order fills and the trade is profitable? Give a decimal.

hints.text: Which path ends in a profitable fill?
The path runs Filled, then Profit.
Multiply along it: $0.6 \times 0.45$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply along the path Filled, then Profit.

byKey.unconditional: You used 0.52, the chance for a buy made on any day. The branch after Filled is conditional on a fill: 0.45.
byKey.branch: That is the second branch alone. Multiply by 0.6, the chance the order fills.
byKey.added: You added along the path. Chances along a path multiply.
byKey.fill-only: That is the chance of a fill. The fill must also be profitable.

explain.text: The path Filled, then Profit gives $0.6 \times 0.45 = 0.27$. Using the day's 0.52 would give 0.312 and overstate the edge, because fills arrive on worse days. That gap is adverse selection, and it is why the second branch must be conditional.

ideas: A tree lays out a sequence: each path from the start to a leaf is one outcome.
Branches after the first stage are conditional, counted on what their path has left.
Multiply along a path, and check the leaves add to 1. A zero branch can be pruned.

formula.name: Path probability
formula.note: Multiply along a path. The leaves of a tree add to 1.

summary.trap: Second-stage branches carry conditional chances, not the first-stage ones again. Leaves that add to 1 do not prove a tree right.

quiz.prose: Over a year, a BBB-rated bond is downgraded with chance 0.08. A downgraded bond then defaults within a year with chance 0.05.
quiz.question: What is the chance the bond is downgraded and then defaults? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of a downgrade, then default

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply along the path downgrade, then default.

byKey.branch: That is the default branch alone, given a downgrade. Multiply by 0.08.
byKey.added: You added along the path. Chances along a path multiply.

explain.text: The path is downgrade, then default. Its chance is $0.08 \times 0.05 = 0.004$, or 4 bonds in 1,000.

quiz.prose: Two cards are dealt from a standard deck without replacement. On the tree, a second-stage branch Heart hangs off a first-stage branch Heart.
quiz.question: Which number belongs on that second-stage branch?

options.why: That is the chance before any card is dealt. The branch hangs off a heart, so one heart is gone.
You took a card out of the deck but not out of the hearts. The card dealt was a heart.
That is the leaf, the product along the path. The branch carries only the second chance.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count what is left after a heart is dealt.

explain.text: The branch is conditional on a heart first. That leaves 12 hearts among 51 cards, so it carries $\tfrac{12}{51}$. The leaf is $\tfrac{13}{52} \times \tfrac{12}{51} = \tfrac{1}{17}$.

quiz.prose: A tree for two trades in a row has four leaves. Three of them are 0.42, 0.18 and 0.28.
quiz.question: What is the fourth leaf? Give a decimal.

widget.label: The fourth leaf
widget.accept: 0.12, since the four leaves add to 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The four leaves of a tree add to 1.

byKey.sum: That is the total of the three leaves you have. The fourth is what is missing from 1.
byKey.one-leaf: You took one leaf from 1. Take all three.

explain.text: The leaves of a tree add to 1. The three you have add to 0.88, so the fourth is $1 - 0.88 = 0.12$.

quiz.prose: A bag holds 3 red counters and 1 blue. Two are drawn, one after the other, without replacement.
quiz.question: Which path has chance 0, so it can be pruned from the tree?

options.why: After a red, 2 reds are left among 3. This path has chance $\tfrac{3}{4} \times \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{1}{2}$.
The blue counter is still in the bag after a red: $\tfrac{3}{4} \times \tfrac{1}{3} = \tfrac{1}{4}$.
After the blue, every counter left is red: $\tfrac{1}{4} \times 1 = \tfrac{1}{4}$.

feedback.correct: Only one blue counter exists, so it cannot come out twice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a path that needs a counter the bag no longer has.

explain.text: After the blue counter, the bag holds only reds, so blue, then blue has chance $\tfrac{1}{4} \times 0 = 0$. The other three paths add to $\tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{1}{4} = 1$, so nothing is lost by pruning it.
